VIGO 1.0.0-rc.2 · Apache-2.0

VIGO 1.0.0-rc.2Open-source transit routing you can explain

Build a network. Answer a transport question.

VIGO 1.0.0-rc.2 turns GTFS timetables and OpenStreetMap streets into a reusable City, then answers three questions about it: how to make a journey, how long every trip takes, and how far people can get. It runs on your own machine, explains each answer, and never needs an internet connection to route.

Build your first CityInstallHTTP API
  • OfflineNo network access at query time
  • One CityBuilt once, opened by every runtime
  • v1 schemasStable public Results
  • Apache-2.0Open source

Start here

  • Build your first CityDownload Boston's public timetable and streets, build a City, and plan a trip from Harvard Square to South Station.
  • Install VIGOPick the engine, the City compiler, the desktop Studio, or the Python package.
  • Serve an HTTP APIAnswer Route, Matrix, and Reach requests from one executable with no runtime dependencies.
  • Analyze in PythonRun batches and notebooks against a City, then export journey and leg tables.

Three questions, one City

QueryIt answersRead more
RouteHow do I travel between these places, and what happens on the way?Route
MatrixHow long does each origin–destination pair take?Matrix
ReachWhere can I get within 15, 30, or 45 minutes?Reach

A Scenario changes the service one query sees, such as a new line or a removed route, so you can measure a proposal against today's network. Compare sets two saved Results side by side without routing again.

Choose your interface

InterfaceBest forWhat it needs
Engine (vigo)Queries, resident streams, and the HTTP APIOne native executable; no Node, Python, or network access
Compiler (vigo.mjs)Building Cities and scenario collections; it can also query themNode.js 24.18 or newer, its bundled native kernel, and the native executable for queries
StudioInspecting service, planning journeys, and exploring Reach and scenariosThe desktop application and its own project library
Python (import vigo)Studies, batches, notebooks, and journey tablesA platform wheel with a headless engine

The engine, the compiler, and Python open the same City directories. For the same City and request, the engine and the compiler return the same public JSON Result.

Built to be explained

Every answer carries its evidence. A Route Result says whether each walk follows mapped streets or a schematic station link. A Matrix keeps unreachable pairs null, never zero. A Reach surface records its grid so that two runs can be compared cell by cell. Known limits state plainly what the model does not establish.

  • Transfer correctness. Fast scans and exceptional transfer searches share the same restrictions. See transfer search and its conservative guards.
  • Stable data. Compatible prepared Cities stay readable in V1 without rebuilding. See the prepared-data contract.
  • Stable results. The public vigo.route.v1, vigo.matrix.v1, and vigo.reach.v1 schemas only gain optional fields. See Read a Result.
  • Offline by default. Queries never fetch anything. This guide works offline too: press / to search, and open saved Results in the Result viewer.

What's new in 1.0.0-rc.2

Opt-in GTFS Flex now joins fixed service in one search: Flex can bring you to a train, take you home from it, or both, and deviated routes keep their scheduled fixed stops. Wheelchair Cities can infer step-free access on ordinary pedestrian ways even when accessibility or surface tags are missing. Read the release notes and the changelog.

Get started

Install VIGO

2 min readSource

On this page

EngineCompilerBuild from sourceName the commandsStudio and PythonSupported platforms

VIGO has four entry points. Most projects use two of them together: the compiler builds a City once from raw data, and the engine answers queries from that City for as long as you like.

You want toInstallRequirements
Query a prepared City or serve HTTPEngine archive (VIGO-Rust-…)Nothing else at query time
Build Cities from GTFS and OSMCompiler archive (CLI)Node.js 24.18 or newer
Explore networks visuallyVIGO StudioThe desktop application
Script analyses and notebooksVIGO PythonPython and the wheel for your platform

Download archives from VIGO releases. Each archive targets one operating system and CPU; City data moves freely between the supported 64-bit targets.

Engine

Extract the engine archive and check the executable:

./vigo --version
./vigo capabilities --pretty
.\vigo.exe --version
.\vigo.exe capabilities --pretty

The executable contains the routing kernels, the City loader, the JSON interface, the HTTP server, and SQLite. It needs no compiler, Node, Python, browser, or internet connection to answer a query. The archive also contains this guide, the OpenAPI document, the engine manual, an audit record, licenses, and a manifest.json that hashes every file.

Compiler

The compiler archive contains vigo.mjs, its matching native routing kernel, license notices, and a checksum manifest. Keep vigo.mjs and vigo-routing-kernel.node in the same directory, then check it with Node.js 24.18 or newer:

Shell
node vigo.mjs --version
node vigo.mjs capabilities

The compiler builds Cities and scenario collections, and runs Route, Matrix, Reach, Stream, and Compare against them. It does not bundle Node or City data. The same steps ship inside the archive as its README.

Build from source

Use Node.js 24.18 or newer, npm 11.6 or newer, the Rust toolchain pinned in rust-toolchain.toml, and a C toolchain for the bundled SQLite. Build natively on the operating system and CPU that will run VIGO:

Shell
git clone https://github.com/hytangs/vigo.git
cd vigo
npm ci
npm run build:cli-runtime
npm run build:standalone

build:cli-runtime produces the compiler, public/vigo.mjs, and its native kernel. build:standalone produces the engine at target/release/vigo. npm run build additionally compiles Studio, and npm run studio opens it.

Name the commands

The guides call the engine vigo and the compiler vigo-build. In a POSIX shell:

Shell
alias vigo="/absolute/path/to/vigo"
alias vigo-build='node "/absolute/path/to/vigo.mjs"'

From a source checkout, point them at target/release/vigo and public/vigo.mjs. On Windows, use .\vigo.exe and node .\vigo.mjs, or define your own functions. Both commands accept --name value and --name=value and reject unknown options.

Studio and Python

VIGO Studio is the desktop workspace. It imports GTFS and OSM into its own project library and opens this guide offline under Settings → Documentation. See the Studio guide.

VIGO Python is versioned separately. Install the wheel for your platform, then follow your first Python query.

Supported platforms

  • macOS 13.5 or newer on Apple Silicon, Linux with glibc on ARM64 and x64, and Windows x64. Linux release builds use Ubuntu 24.04. There are no 32-bit or native Windows ARM64 binaries.
  • The engine container image runs on Debian with glibc. See Deploy the routing engine.
  • Studio maps require WebGL 2. The engine, the compiler, and Python need no graphics device.

Quickstart: Boston in ten minutes

5 min readSource

On this page

1. Download the Boston inputs2. Build the City3. Plan a journey4. Read the Result5. Compute a matrix6. Map where you can go7. Keep the City loadedWhere next

In about ten minutes you will build a City for Boston and Cambridge from public data, then plan a journey from Harvard Square to South Station, compute a small matrix, and map where you can reach in 45 minutes. A City is the prepared data directory, here ./boston.

You need the engine and the compiler, named vigo and vigo-build, plus curl, unzip, and Osmium Tool. The commands use a POSIX shell; on Windows, use WSL for the download and extract steps.

Tip

Every request below works with either runtime. Replace vigo with vigo-build to run a query through the compiler instead; the Result is the same.

1. Download the Boston inputs

Two files supply different parts of a journey:

DataOfficial sourceWhat VIGO uses it for
MBTA static GTFS ZIPMBTA GTFS documentation, download ZIPStops, trips, calendars, transfers, fares, and transit shapes
Massachusetts OpenStreetMap PBFGeofabrik Massachusetts, download PBFStreets for walking access, egress, transfers, walking, and driving

No API key is needed. Choose the static GTFS ZIP, not GTFS-realtime, and the .osm.pbf, not a shapefile or GeoPackage.

Shell
mkdir -p boston-tutorial/data
cd boston-tutorial
curl --fail --location --retry 3 --output data/MBTA_GTFS.zip \
  https://cdn.mbta.com/MBTA_GTFS.zip
curl --fail --location --retry 3 --output data/massachusetts-latest.osm.pbf \
  https://download.geofabrik.de/north-america/us/massachusetts-latest.osm.pbf
unzip -p data/MBTA_GTFS.zip feed_info.txt
unzip -p data/MBTA_GTFS.zip calendar.txt

feed_start_date and feed_end_date give the published interval. The feed checked for this tutorial covers 2026-09-25 through 2026-12-12, and the examples use Monday 2026-10-05. With a later download, choose a date inside its interval and check calendar.txt and calendar_dates.txt: a date inside the interval does not mean every route runs that day. Times are local MBTA service times in America/New_York.

2. Build the City

Cut a smaller street extract around central Boston and Cambridge, then build:

Shell
osmium extract --bbox=-71.20,42.25,-70.95,42.45 --strategy=complete_ways \
  data/massachusetts-latest.osm.pbf --output=data/boston.osm.pbf
vigo-build build --gtfs ./data/MBTA_GTFS.zip --osm ./data/boston.osm.pbf \
  --output ./boston --prepare-date 2026-10-05
vigo info --city ./boston --pretty

The complete-ways strategy keeps every node of the ways crossing the rectangle. This extract covers the tutorial's places, not street access for the whole MBTA network; for a wider study, enlarge it or pass the full Massachusetts PBF. --prepare-date precompiles that day's timetable so that a fresh engine process can reuse it. Keep the providers' notices when you share data; see OpenStreetMap attribution.

VIGO writes one complete ./boston directory and leaves an existing output alone unless you pass --replace. vigo info confirms the City's name, revision, sources, and warnings. Keep the whole directory: the inspection output identifies the City but contains no routing data.

3. Plan a journey

Save route.json. Coordinates are [longitude, latitude]:

JSON
{
  "origin": {"coordinate": [-71.11902, 42.37334]},
  "destination": {"coordinate": [-71.05524, 42.35227]},
  "serviceDate": "2026-10-05",
  "time": "08:00",
  "maxWalkKm": 1.2,
  "maxTransfers": 3,
  "requireTransitRide": true
}
Shell
vigo route --city ./boston --request route.json
vigo route --city ./boston --request route.json --output route-result.json

In a terminal, the first command prints a short itinerary. The second saves the full JSON Result. To ask when to leave to arrive by 09:00, override the clock and time direction:

vigo route --city ./boston --request route.json --time 09:00 --arrive-by
vigo-build route --city ./boston --request route.json --time 09:00 --time-preference arrive

Command-line flags override fields in the request file. In JSON, the same choice is "time": "09:00", "timePreference": "arrive_by", which both runtimes accept.

4. Read the Result

Read status first. ok contains a journey; not_found is a valid answer meaning no journey satisfies the date, walking limit, transfer cap, and time horizon you asked for. Then read journey.departureTime, journey.arrivalTime, and the ordered journey.legs. Clocks are local service-day HH:MM:SS; durations are integer seconds.

Trip IDs and times depend on the feed you downloaded, and this is scheduled routing without live delays. Check warnings and each walk's quality before treating a path as a passenger-facing guarantee; walking evidence explains station costs and schematic links. Open route-result.json in the Result viewer to see the journey as a timeline.

5. Compute a matrix

Save matrix.json. The rows are Harvard Square and Kendall Square; the columns are South Station and Copley Square:

JSON
{
  "origins": [
    {"id": "harvard", "coordinate": [-71.11902, 42.37334]},
    {"id": "kendall", "coordinate": [-71.08618, 42.36249]}
  ],
  "destinations": [
    {"id": "south-station", "coordinate": [-71.05524, 42.35227]},
    {"id": "copley", "coordinate": [-71.07758, 42.34997]}
  ],
  "serviceDate": "2026-10-05",
  "time": "08:00",
  "maxWalkKm": 1.2,
  "maxTransfers": 3,
  "includeJourneys": true
}
Shell
vigo matrix --city ./boston --request matrix.json --output matrix-result.json

Read durationsSeconds[origin][destination] in request order, and the matching journeys entry when requested. An unreachable pair is null, never zero. Repeated origins or destinations share work internally, and every requested cell is still returned.

6. Map where you can go

Save reach.json to find the streets and areas reachable from Harvard Square within 15, 30, and 45 minutes:

JSON
{
  "origin": {"coordinate": [-71.11902, 42.37334]},
  "serviceDate": "2026-10-05",
  "time": "08:00",
  "cutoffsMinutes": [15, 30, 45],
  "extentRadiusKm": 6,
  "rasterSize": 48
}
Shell
vigo reach --city ./boston --request reach.json --output reach-result.json

surface.valuesSeconds is a row-major raster from the northwest corner, and areas holds GeoJSON polygons for each cutoff. A Reach surface describes modeled travel time; it is not a count of jobs or people. See Reach for resolution, sampling, and comparison rules.

7. Keep the City loaded

One-off commands open the City every time. For repeated work, keep one process resident. Save queries.ndjson with one request per line:

NDJSON
{"id":"harvard-south-depart","kind":"route","origin":{"coordinate":[-71.11902,42.37334]},"destination":{"coordinate":[-71.05524,42.35227]},"serviceDate":"2026-10-05","time":"08:00","maxWalkKm":1.2,"maxTransfers":3}
{"id":"harvard-south-arrive","kind":"route","origin":{"coordinate":[-71.11902,42.37334]},"destination":{"coordinate":[-71.05524,42.35227]},"serviceDate":"2026-10-05","time":"09:00","timePreference":"arrive_by","maxWalkKm":1.2,"maxTransfers":3}
Shell
vigo stream --city ./boston < queries.ndjson > results.ndjson

Each output line echoes its id; check every status, because one failed line does not end the stream. To serve applications over HTTP, start the engine's service and call it from a second terminal:

Shell
vigo serve --city ./boston --port 8080
curl --fail-with-body http://127.0.0.1:8080/v1/route \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' --data-binary @route.json

Open http://127.0.0.1:8080/ to read this guide from the running service, and send requests from the API console at the end of the HTTP API page. When you measure performance, keep the City build, a fresh process's first answer, and requests to a resident process separate.

Core concepts

4 min readSource

On this page

CityScenarioQueryResultChoose a supported combinationOutcomesTime

VIGO has four nouns and three questions. Once these are clear, every interface behaves the way you expect.

GTFS + OSM ──build──▶ City ──(optional Scenario)──▶ Route | Matrix | Reach ──▶ Result

City

A City is a compiled mobility model built from GTFS and OSM. It is one complete directory, so its timetable, streets, and prepared query data cannot drift apart. Rebuilding from new source data creates a new City revision; existing Scenarios and Results stay tied to the revision that produced them. revisionId identifies the immutable build, builtAt records when it was made, and sources records the GTFS and OSM inputs.

A built City reopens without its raw GTFS or OSM files. Building prepares the street indexes and station-access state. The first query for a new set of active services prepares a timetable snapshot that later processes can reload; dates with the same active services share it, and --prepare-date creates it ahead of time. A new process still loads the files into memory, while a resident process keeps them ready.

Prepared files are tied to the source revision, routing policy, and format. Missing, stale, or incompatible timetable and access caches are rebuilt from the compiled City without importing raw sources again. Required street files must remain complete: restore or rebuild a City with missing or corrupt street indexes. Updating the underlying GTFS or OSM data requires a new build.

Scenario

A Scenario is an immutable set of changes applied to one City revision. Planned service changes apply to Reach. Supplied traffic applies to Drive Route and Drive Matrix, and a supplied realtime snapshot applies to transit Route; requests carry these as scenario, traffic, and realtimeSnapshot. Walking limits, departure times, and cutoffs remain query options. A complete alternative GTFS source is a new City revision, not a Scenario.

VIGO rejects unsupported combinations before computing. It never silently drops a change or moves a Scenario to a newer City revision. See Scenarios.

Query

QueryWhat it computesNotes
RouteTravel between ordered points, with legs, transfers, and walkingDepart-at or arrive-by; waypoints, alternatives, and departure windows are Route options
MatrixScalar travel time between sets of origins and destinationsA single origin is a one-row Matrix; journeys are optional
ReachWhere the network can take you within stated time limitsShown as reached streets, areas, or contours

Depart-at minimizes arrival time, then boardings, then walking. Arrive-by maximizes departure time; among journeys leaving at that boundary and arriving by the deadline, it minimizes boardings, walking, and actual arrival.

Reach is not accessibility. An accessibility measure also needs opportunities such as jobs, people, schools, or health care, and a stated way to combine them.

Result

A Result is the immutable answer to one Query: status, values, warnings, timing, the City revision, the Scenario if any, and the query output. Compare is an action on two compatible Results, not a fourth query. Keep the original request and the full Result together; the normalized query echo is useful for inspection but is not a complete archive of every option or supplied observation. See Read a Result.

Choose a supported combination

QueryTravel modeTime constraintSupplied changes or observations
RouteTransitDepart-at or arrive-by; waypoints and departure windows have their own limitsMatched GTFS-RT Trip Updates when realtime is explicitly selected
RouteWalk or DriveStreet routing with the chosen time directionSupplied traffic for Drive in realtime mode
MatrixTransitFixed departure or arrival deadlineScheduled timetable only
MatrixWalk or DriveStatic street metric; arrive-by does not introduce time-varying trafficSupplied traffic for Drive in realtime mode
ReachTransit with walking, or WalkFixed departure and time cutoffsPlanned-service Scenario; scheduled analysis

vigo capabilities describes the running build. Queries default to scheduled mode. Drive traffic needs both the traffic object and an explicit routingDataMode: "realtime"; VIGO never fetches a traffic provider. A visible vehicle, alert, or added trip is not itself a routing update.

Outcomes

  • Public Route and Reach Results use ok or not_found. A completed Matrix is ok, with null for unreachable cells.
  • Invalid or unsupported requests fail with an error and a nonzero exit code, or HTTP 4xx. Execution failures are errors too, never analysis Results.
  • Python Results use ready and blocked; those names belong to the Python API.
  • Studio background tasks report queued, running, ready, cancelled, or error.

Time

Service dates use the City's timetable timezone. A GTFS event at 25:10 belongs to the service date it was published on, even though it happens after midnight. Request clocks may exceed 24 hours, so always supply the exact service date with the clock. Realtime observation timestamps are a separate clock used only to admit or reject predictions.

VIGO keeps Build, Open, Compute, and End-to-end durations separate. Reusing an open process is useful runtime behavior; it does not hide or replace query computation.

Practical workflows

4 min readSource

On this page

Choose a queryExplain one journeyReach one destination by a deadlineTest a planned service changeInvestigate live service

These recipes start from the quickstart City, ./boston, and its coordinates. Each JSON block is a complete request to save under the filename shown. Replace the date with one your feed covers.

Choose a query

QuestionUseRead
How can someone make this journey?RouteTimed legs, transfers, walking, and access qualifications
When must people leave to reach one place by a deadline?Arrive-by MatrixPer-pair duration and departure; optional actual journey arrival
Where can someone travel within a time budget?ReachGrid values and areas at the chosen cutoffs
How would a proposed service change that reach?Baseline Reach, Scenario Reach, then CompareTime changes and newly or no-longer-reachable cells
What are the live feeds reporting now?Studio NetworkObservation time, coverage, predictions, and source identity

The support table shows which modes and supplied states each query accepts.

Explain one journey

Save journey.json:

JSON
{
  "origin": {"coordinate": [-71.11902, 42.37334]},
  "destination": {"coordinate": [-71.08337, 42.32978]},
  "serviceDate": "2026-10-05",
  "time": "08:00",
  "mode": "transit",
  "maxWalkKm": 1.2
}
Shell
vigo route --city ./boston --request journey.json --output journey-result.json

Check status, then the chronological journey.legs. Walking competes with transit, so a short trip can return a walk; set requireTransitRide: true to require a boarding, or "mode": "walk" to request walking alone. A not_found Result can reflect the date, timetable, access network, or constraints. It does not mean the places are physically disconnected; Troubleshooting lists the checks in order.

For several journeys at the requested time, add "alternatives": 3. The default pareto ranking keeps only genuine trade-offs between arrival, boardings, and walking; "alternativeRanking": "ranked" lists the earliest distinct journeys even when one beats another in every respect. Equal-arrival ranked journeys prefer less walking, then fewer boardings; the least-walking returned tie becomes the primary journey. See alternative journeys and journey windows.

Reach one destination by a deadline

Save arrival-matrix.json:

JSON
{
  "origins": [
    {"id": "harvard", "coordinate": [-71.11902, 42.37334]},
    {"id": "central", "coordinate": [-71.1035, 42.3654]}
  ],
  "destinations": [
    {"id": "destination", "coordinate": [-71.08337, 42.32978]}
  ],
  "serviceDate": "2026-10-05",
  "time": "09:00",
  "timePreference": "arrive_by",
  "includeJourneys": true
}
Shell
vigo matrix --city ./boston --request arrival-matrix.json --output arrival-matrix-result.json

Every pair shares the deadline. durationsSeconds[origin][destination] runs from the latest feasible departure to the deadline, so it can include waiting at the destination; the matching journeys entry gives the actual modeled departure, arrival, walking, waiting, and transfers. Set includeJourneys to false when only times are needed. A shared destination and deadline share one reverse search, and a shared origin and departure share one forward search. Split larger jobs by shared time and options; see Matrix for limits.

Test a planned service change

Save baseline-reach.json:

JSON
{
  "origin": {"coordinate": [-71.11902, 42.37334]},
  "serviceDate": "2026-10-05",
  "time": "08:00",
  "maxWalkKm": 1.2,
  "cutoffsMinutes": [15, 30, 45],
  "extentRadiusKm": 6,
  "rasterSize": 48
}

Save alternative-reach.json with the same origin and surface settings plus a Scenario:

JSON
{
  "origin": {"coordinate": [-71.11902, 42.37334]},
  "serviceDate": "2026-10-05",
  "time": "08:00",
  "maxWalkKm": 1.2,
  "cutoffsMinutes": [15, 30, 45],
  "extentRadiusKm": 6,
  "rasterSize": 48,
  "scenario": {
    "id": "direct-service",
    "name": "Illustrative direct service",
    "services": [{
      "operation": "add",
      "name": "Direct service",
      "stops": [
        {"label": "Origin", "coordinate": [-71.11902, 42.37334]},
        {"label": "Destination", "coordinate": [-71.08337, 42.32978]}
      ],
      "headwayMinutes": 10,
      "startMinutes": 420,
      "endMinutes": 600,
      "averageSpeedKph": 20
    }]
  }
}

The speed, headway, and operating span are illustrative. The example uses the defaults of bidirectional service, distance-estimated timing, and 0.35-minute dwell. It does not establish a drivable alignment, achievable running time, vehicle requirement, or service plan; Scenarios explains how to specify a real proposal.

Run both, then compare the saved Results with the compiler:

Shell
vigo reach --city ./boston --request baseline-reach.json --output baseline-result.json
vigo reach --city ./boston --request alternative-reach.json --output alternative-result.json
vigo-build compare --before ./baseline-result.json --after ./alternative-result.json \
  --output ./reach-change.json

Compare uses the retained surfaces. counts splits cells reachable in both into faster, slower, and unchanged, and counts newly and no-longer-reachable cells separately; a negative meanChangeSeconds means faster modeled travel among the comparable cells. Read all the counts together. A larger area is not a population benefit: an accessibility study also needs opportunity data, a spatial assignment method, and an explicit measure. The engine's vigo compare takes both Results in one request; see Compare saved Reach results.

Investigate live service

In Studio, start in Network: check the observation time and reporting coverage, then choose a route in Routes. Compare scheduled and predicted events at the same stop, and inspect a vehicle's position separately from its stop-time predictions.

Use Route → Realtime to query supported, matched predictions. A vehicle on the map, an alert, or an added trip in Trip times does not by itself make that service available to routing. See Network and Routes and realtime admission.

For a reproducible analysis, use an exact date and time in Scheduled mode. For an incident review, retain the observation, identity, coverage, and Result from the original investigation. Read a Result covers both.

Cities and data

Build a City

3 min readSource

On this page

Choose inputsBuild optionsLarge regions and low memoryCopy and load a CityUpdate a networkScenario collections

A City is compiled once by vigo-build and then opened read-only by any number of engine processes, Python sessions, or compiler queries. This chapter covers inputs, build options, and the life cycle of a City. The quickstart shows a complete Boston build.

Choose inputs

InputRequirement
GTFSOne or more static GTFS ZIP files. Repeat --gtfs for several feeds and give each a stable --gtfs-scope; see multiple feeds.
OSMOne .osm.pbf covering every origin, destination, stop access, and transfer location you will query.

Keep the original files, their checksums, and their acquisition date. Download URLs such as latest are not frozen datasets. GTFS support lists the source features VIGO reads and the ones it reports as unsupported.

Build options

Shell
vigo-build build --gtfs feed.zip --osm region.osm.pbf --output ./city
vigo-build inspect --city ./city
OptionEffect
--prepare-date YYYY-MM-DDPrecompile a service date's timetable; repeat for other dates
--street-modes walkBuild walking only and omit all driving data
--private-access endpointsAllow mapped private paths at trip endpoints; see authorized endpoint access
--wheelchairBuild a strict wheelchair City; see wheelchair routing
--wheelchair-streetsinferred (default) can assume ordinary pedestrian ways are step-free when wheelchair or surface tags are missing; verified uses only wheelchair=yes ways
--streets-from ./other-cityReuse identical immutable streets from a prepared City
--replaceReplace an existing output; without it, an existing City is left alone

Build is staged: a failed build preserves the previous City, and --replace restores the previous directory if publication fails. A successful replacement removes its temporary backup, so use a separate output directory when you need a rollback copy.

Raw import and street preparation happen at build time and are separate from query latency.

Large regions and low memory

Builds use disk-backed SQLite temporary work and compact numeric node lookups, report progress during long import phases, and respect container memory limits when deciding whether GTFS and OSM compilation may overlap. Import and native street preparation run in separate processes, so each stage releases its working memory before the next. Keep the output and temporary directory on a local filesystem (inside WSL, prefer the Linux filesystem to /mnt/c), and leave space for the source database, temporary sorts, and the finished City.

Regional native CCH preprocessing can still exceed 2 GiB without swap. Configure disk-backed swap for the build machine, or build on a larger machine and copy the complete City to the server: build memory and query memory are separate requirements. Street preparation must write the walking accelerator before the graph is sealed, so a City that could not open is never published.

Copy and load a City

A City contains network.json, routing/project.sqlite, prepared access artifacts, and an osm directory with street snapshots, access profiles, and CCH indexes. Exact member names can vary with the preparation version. Copy the whole directory, never just the SQLite files or the manifest.

The engine checks source identities, snapshot formats, station and access profiles, and required CCH members. It rejects blocking source features, missing or stale preparations, and an unexpected SQLite WAL. Complete a City through its compiler; do not delete WAL files to bypass validation. The engine reports timing.timetableSource: "prepared_snapshot" when it reuses a prepared timetable and "source" when it prepared one from SQLite for that process. Both use the same schedule.

Update a network

Treat a published City as immutable while any process has it open. Compile updates into a new directory, start another service against it, verify readiness and a known query, switch traffic, and then stop the old service. The engine has no upload endpoint, source downloader, or hot reload. See Upgrade and rollback for version changes.

Scenario collections

When you compare several timetables over one street network, build a scenario collection: one shared street graph, several transit scenarios, and a default. See Shared scenario collections for the source manifest and residency rules.

Cities and data

Combine timetables and live feeds

3 min readSource

On this page

Build a City from multiple GTFS filesConnect multiple GTFS-RT endpointsSupply observations to the engine

A City can contain several static GTFS feeds and several GTFS-Realtime endpoints. Static feeds supply the scheduled network; live feeds supply observations and predictions for it and never replace the timetable.

Build a City from multiple GTFS files

In Studio, open City → Data sources and add each GTFS ZIP. VIGO imports each source, then builds the combined routing store. Add an overlapping OSM PBF for walking, driving, and coordinate-based transit access, and wait for preparation to finish before querying.

With the compiler, repeat --gtfs and give each input a stable, unique scope:

Shell
vigo-build build \
  --gtfs ./rail.zip --gtfs-scope rail \
  --gtfs ./bus.zip --gtfs-scope bus \
  --osm ./region.osm.pbf \
  --output ./city

A scope identifies a source feed, not a route number. The merged store namespaces stops, routes, trips, services, and transfer references so identical IDs in different feeds cannot overwrite one another. Use the same scope names when you rebuild the same sources. Removing a source in Studio rebuilds the surviving combined store.

Before combining feeds:

  • Use compatible service dates. A trip is usable only when its own calendar and exceptions activate it for the requested service day.
  • Keep agencies in one timezone. Cross-timezone routing stores are rejected.
  • Avoid importing two editions of the same agency timetable as separate networks unless that duplication is intentional.
  • Retain declared transfers and verify street coverage. Close coordinates alone do not prove a usable station connection.

Connect multiple GTFS-RT endpoints

  1. Open City → Data sources → GTFS-RT live feeds, or feed settings in Network.
  2. Paste an endpoint URL and choose what it contains. A combined endpoint may contain several entity types.
  3. Select its matching Timetable when the City has several static sources.
  4. Choose Add feed for each additional endpoint, then Connect live.
  5. Expand Feed status to inspect individual failures and freshness.

Live-feed requests use { "sources": [{ "url": "https://operator.example/trip-updates.pb", "kind": "tripUpdates" }] }. The old top-level url and urls formats are rejected; reconnect those saved connections through the feed editor. A single MBTA endpoint no longer implicitly enables the other two.

Trip Updates can be connected without Vehicle Positions. The MBTA preset fills three public endpoints; select the MBTA timetable when you use it in a combined City. A failed endpoint does not discard successful ones. Reimporting or merging a timetable invalidates the retained observation until a fresh fetch binds to the new City, and old records from a failed endpoint are not carried into a new snapshot.

DataWhat VIGO uses it for
Trip UpdatesSupported predictions and cancellations in transit Route; trip and station inspection
Vehicle PositionsReported map locations, vehicle details, and qualified service observations
AlertsScoped notices and evidence; text does not automatically close a route

Studio allows up to 16 distinct endpoints. Repeated URLs for the same timetable are fetched once, and assigning one URL to conflicting timetables is rejected. A refresh has a 30-second overall deadline, a 20 MB per-feed limit, and a 40 MB combined limit. Batches also reject more than 200,000 entities or 500,000 stop predictions. At most four downloads run concurrently, and oversized or failed sources are disclosed individually.

The declared type is descriptive: every supported entity present in the protobuf is decoded. A source timestamp and timetable identity travel with each record. Unscoped IDs match only when unambiguous; a bare trip ID never resolves by choosing the first agency.

Supply observations to the engine

Neither command-line runtime opens feed URLs. A Route request can carry a retained, normalized realtimeSnapshot with routingDataMode: "realtime". In a combined City, each record can carry sourceScope equal to its build scope, alongside the original tripId, sourceFeedTimestamp, service date, and stop predictions. A single-source City uses raw GTFS IDs; omit sourceScope there. The realtime input reference lists every record field.

Keep source timestamps intact. Changing a capture's timestamps to make it look current changes the input and is not a replay of that observation. A repeated snapshot ages out of the routing cache.

Scenario collections

1 min readSource

A collection serves several transit scenarios against one immutable street graph. Prepare it with node public/vigo.mjs build-scenarios --spec scenarios.source.json --output scenario-set, then point vigo serve --city scenario-set or vigo stream --city scenario-set at the result. Each request selects a scenarioId; omission selects defaultScenario. The one-shot CLI also accepts --scenario ID.

For populations authorized to enter their own homes and destinations on mapped private roads, set "privateAccess": "endpoints" in the scenario source specification. Every member then receives an endpoint-only access overlay; private streets cannot become public through shortcuts. Endpoint overlays use each member's transit anchors, so these collections currently retain separate street directories. The default "public" policy keeps the shared street directory. This does not enlarge coordinate snapping or invent paths for unmapped endpoints. Wheelchair collections require public access.

For wheelchair routing, add "wheelchair": true to the source specification or pass build-scenarios --wheelchair. Every member and the shared street graph then use wheelchair-strict-v1; unknown accessibility is excluded. Wheelchair collections require streetModes: "walk". Conflicting CLI/spec values and non-boolean specification values are rejected before compilation. Use a separate regular collection when both profiles are needed.

JSON
{
  "schemaVersion": "vigo.scenarios.source.v1",
  "name": "Regional alternatives",
  "osm": { "path": "region.osm.pbf" },
  "streetModes": "walk",
  "prepareDates": ["2026-10-05"],
  "defaultScenario": "baseline",
  "maximumResidentScenarios": 2,
  "scenarios": [
    { "id": "baseline", "name": "Baseline", "feeds": [{ "path": "baseline.zip", "scope": "agency" }] },
    { "id": "proposal", "name": "Proposal", "feeds": [{ "path": "proposal.zip", "scope": "agency" }] }
  ]
}

Source paths are relative to the manifest. Optional sha256 values pin each input. The compiler prepares street data once and creates relative references to it. Move the collection as one directory. Its checksum inventory records physical files once. prepareDates precompiles up to 32 service dates, reusing identical service sets; other dates remain queryable through the source timetable. A single-City build accepts repeated --prepare-date options.

Wheelchair routing

5 min readSource

On this page

Native planner integrationBatched place names

Prepare a separate wheelchair City with the preparation CLI:

Shell
vigo build --gtfs feed.zip --osm region.osm.pbf --output wheelchair-city --wheelchair

The Engine CLI and HTTP service use that City for Route, Matrix and Reach. Add "wheelchair": true to the request, or --wheelchair to an Engine CLI query. Omitting the option inherits the City's profile. Ordinary Cities reject a true request; wheelchair Cities reject false, Drive, realtime transit and query-time scenario overlays. Expanded-walking choices are suppressed for this profile, including when the wheelchair flag is omitted. Compile changed inputs into a new wheelchair City. Serve the prepared wheelchair City using the same serve --city wheelchair-city command and authenticated /v1/route, /v1/matrix and /v1/reach endpoints.

Studio's Route settings also expose Wheelchair routing. Prepare a separate wheelchair City from the exact GTFS ZIP and OSM PBF imported into your Studio City, then attach it from the source checkout:

Shell
node scripts/attach-studio-wheelchair.mjs /path/to/Studio-City /path/to/wheelchair-city

Restart Studio after attaching or replacing the network. Attachment checks the source fingerprints and profile, preserves the ordinary City, and retains any previous wheelchair network as a backup. Studio currently supports this profile for single-feed, scheduled Route queries without via points or scenario overlays; use the Engine CLI for wheelchair Matrix and Reach. Unknown vehicle and boarding accessibility is excluded; inferred streets can have unknown accessibility. A missing, incomplete or source-mismatched wheelchair network returns an error; it never silently substitutes an unrestricted route. The option does not certify elevator operation or access between a building and the street.

The wheelchair-strict-v1 profile requires GTFS wheelchair_accessible=1 for vehicles and wheelchair_boarding=1 for boarding/alighting, including published parent inheritance. An accessible vehicle can pass an inaccessible stop without boarding or alighting. Unknown values are excluded. Search considers accessible alternatives directly, including later vehicles; it does not filter a completed unrestricted journey.

Street evidence is chosen at build time with --wheelchair-streets and reported as accessibility.streetEvidence on every result:

ValueBuild optionOSM ways used
inferred-step-free-v1default, or --wheelchair-streets inferredOrdinary pedestrian ways, including ways without a surface or wheelchair tag, subject to the filters below
wheelchair-yes-only--wheelchair-streets verifiedOnly ways tagged wheelchair=yes

For inferred evidence without wheelchair=yes, rough surfaces, bad smoothness, mountain trail grades and paths, tracks or bridleways without a mapped paved surface are excluded. An explicit wheelchair=yes overrides those surface and trail filters. Both policies require ordinary pedestrian permission and exclude steps, escalators, mapped inaccessible or limited nodes, raised kerbs and conditional accessibility. Published widths below 0.9 m and inclines above 8.3% are excluded. A mapped kerb must be lowered or flush. Inferred evidence passes unlocked gates and bollards; other barriers need wheelchair=yes. Untagged shape vertices inherit the way's accessibility. These are fixed profile limits, not a personalized chair model. Although accessibility.unknownData is exclude, the inferred street policy can admit ways whose wheelchair or surface tags are unknown; check accessibility.streetEvidence and the limitations. Inferred streets are not surveyed: few cities tag every sidewalk, so verified evidence alone usually leaves little or no network.

Station paths require either a positive published wheelchair_traversal_time (the MBTA extension) or step-free mode with published width at least 0.9 m, slope at most 0.083 in magnitude and a traversal cost. Elevator paths do not require slope. Explicit stairs and escalators remain excluded even if a contradictory wheelchair time is present. Direction is preserved. Missing paths do not generate parent-station shortcuts. Generic transfer recommendations do not establish accessible paths. For transit access, station platforms are reached from declared accessible entrances and paths, rather than snapped directly from the street.

Every successful or no-route response carries accessibility, including the profile, its street evidence and its limitations. Coordinate-to-network attachments are geometric; door-to-street access is not verified. Live elevator outages, temporary barriers and individual chair dimensions are not modeled. Strict source requirements can leave sparse coverage or no route. A no-route result is not evidence that no accessible real-world trip exists.

Source semantics: GTFS Schedule, MBTA pathways, and OSM wheelchair tags. The public synthetic regression is npm run check:wheelchair; it checks accessible alternatives through both CLIs and authenticated HTTP, as well as Matrix, Reach, reverse routing and profile mismatch rejection.

Native planner integration

Clients can request journeyPolicy: "alternatives-v1" on transit Route. Capabilities exposes route.journeyPolicies; deployment checks should require this value before switching an adapter. The policy returns the ordinary vigo.route.v1 journey and alternatives, preserving direct transit and a permitted direct walk. It orders by arrival (departure for arrive-by), then walking and boardings. Journeys sharing the same boarding/alighting stations, modes and walking policy are bundled; GTFS parent-station identifiers determine station membership. Do not combine it with explicit alternatives, windows or via points. Arrive-by retains a 15-minute earlier-arrival window sampled every five minutes.

expandedWalkKm is explicit permission for a wider transit-access search; omit it when the user sets a binding walking limit. A wider choice must beat every ordinary choice on the time objective by at least one minute (earlier arrival, or later departure for arrive-by); walking farther for a shorter but later journey is not offered. In supported windows, a choice whose final ride, with its wait, reaches the destination later than walking on from where the previous ride ends is replaced by that walk, when the walk fits the wider budget and arrives at least a minute sooner. Wider choices carry expandedWalkingLimitKm. A whole-trip walk uses at most maxWalkKm unless allowLongWalk explicitly permits maxStreetKm. Limits below 50 metres do not trigger a widened street query. requireTransitRide excludes walking-only choices. Optional wider-search failures preserve ordinary results.

Use sharedLegs: true for native single-leg substitutions and observed departure frequency. Missing or truncated frequency evidence must remain unknown; it is not a zero headway or a complete route-wide schedule. The client remains responsible for labels, rendering, authentication, cancellation, deadlines and bounded caching. The policy consolidates HTTP requests; it still performs bounded searches inside the resident Rust engine and is not a claim of one algorithm traversal.

Batched place names

POST /v1/native accepts {"operation":"places.describe","input":{"longitudes":[-71.06],"latitudes":[42.36]}}. The result contains parallel labels and kinds arrays in input order, with null entries when no nearby label is available. Batches are limited to 256 coordinates. This uses the same native place index as Studio: optional prepared OSM naming tables and GTFS stops, without an external geocoder. A label is descriptive and does not change the routing coordinate or establish accessibility.

Routing

Route

6 min readSource

On this page

InputsWalking and transitTransfers and time reservesHow a journey is chosenAlternatives and windowsResult and diagnosticsStations, access, and geometry

Route finds and explains travel between ordered points. This chapter describes how Route behaves; the Route request reference lists every field and default.

Inputs

A Route query selects:

  • an origin, optional ordered waypoints, and a destination;
  • transit, walk, or drive;
  • an exact service date and local time;
  • depart-at or arrive-by;
  • a walking limit, an optional maximum number of transfers, and the objective;
  • optional alternatives or a departure window;
  • optional supplied observations supported by the selected mode.

Stop IDs are exact GTFS identifiers. Coordinate points are [longitude, latitude] and need streets in the City.

Walking and transit

Transit Route and Matrix compare a direct OSM walk by default, so a short coordinate trip can return walking when it arrives sooner. Set requireTransitRide: true to require at least one boarding, or select Walk mode to request walking alone. maxWalkKm limits each access and egress walk. Set allowLongWalk: false to apply the same limit to a direct walking alternative; otherwise maxStreetKm bounds the complete walk. Explicit Walk mode always uses maxStreetKm, regardless of allowLongWalk, including when maxWalkKm is zero. maxStreetKm accepts 0.05–1000 km; zero and smaller values are rejected rather than rounded up. Clients offering smaller walking limits must enforce their own stricter distance contract.

horizonMinutes sets the timetable search horizon (default 480, range 1–2880). For depart-at transit, boarding and alighting must happen at or before this boundary, including in alternative journeys; the final walk can finish after it. The horizon is therefore not a hard limit on door-to-door duration: comparisons with a total-duration cap must check the final arrival separately. Explicit Walk and Drive routes use maxStreetKm rather than the transit horizon; Walk also ignores the transit-only allowLongWalk restriction.

allowStreetTransfers (default true) controls walking connections between separate stops or stations. Turn it off to change vehicles only at the same stop or between members of one station, as identified by the GTFS station hierarchy. The engine removes cross-station walking edges before searching, including for arrive-by, realtime, and departure-window searches; access to the first stop and egress from the last remain available. Studio exposes this as Route options → Allow walks between stations or stops. It does not certify station-interior paths or free-transfer eligibility.

disableCache: true disables street-access frontier and walking-path caches while keeping the prepared City resident. Route answers are recomputed either way. The same flag applies to the wider access probes used to explain a blocked Route.

Transfers and time reserves

maxTransfers accepts integers from 0 to 31: 0 permits one boarding and 1 permits two. Omit it for no additional cap. Staying aboard the same trip is not a transfer. The cap constrains the native search, including alternatives and arrive-by, so a slower feasible route is found when the unrestricted winner exceeds it. A finite cap with ordered transit waypoints is unsupported.

minimumTransferBufferMinutes (integer 0–60, default 0) adds time before each subsequent boarding, after any transfer walk and the feed's own minimum transfer time. It is charged once per transfer, including a change at the same stop, and never delays the first boarding, the final egress, or staying aboard. arrivalBufferMinutes plans an arrive-by query against an earlier deadline. Both are timetable feasibility constraints, not delay predictions; see Time reserves.

Studio starts with a one-minute transfer buffer after any transfer walk, so a change between different services cannot rely on simultaneous arrival and departure. The first boarding and staying aboard the same trip are unaffected; Preferences can change the buffer, including explicitly selecting none. This reserve is a planning margin, not a guarantee against delay.

The engine API adds no implicit boarding buffer. Same-stop changes honor published GTFS minimum transfer times and forbidden transfers. Explicit transfer edges keep their durations without an added margin or a 60-second floor, and a published platform-to-platform transfer rule takes precedence over the station walking fallback.

How a journey is chosen

VIGO's objective is earliest_arrival. Equal-arrival journeys prefer fewer boardings, then less walking, then a stable final order; there is no undefined "balanced" preference. Arrive-by first maximizes departure time; among journeys leaving at that boundary and arriving by the deadline, it minimizes boardings, then walking, then actual arrival. A slightly later on-time arrival can therefore avoid unnecessary transfers.

If the reverse boundary cannot be materialized at first, the engine reconstructs a forward witness at the same departure from the complete access frontier. A remaining mismatch is a query error; an earlier feasible departure is never reported as the latest. An independently verified direct walk may dominate the reverse transit bound.

Ordered transit routes can walk any segment, including the whole journey. Selection compares complete journeys by arrival (or latest departure), then boardings and walking, so a later walk to a waypoint can replace a short ride when both catch the same onward vehicle. Up to eight partial journeys are retained at each waypoint and up to five complete choices are returned; this bounded search does not enumerate every itinerary. requireTransitRide: true requires a ride on every segment.

Alternatives and windows

alternatives (0–9) asks a depart-at transit Route for more journeys at the requested time; both runtimes return the same list. A departure window instead samples nearby departures: the engine's windowMinutes searches later departures or earlier deadlines, while the compiler's departureWindowMinutes (±0–30) is a centered depart-at profile. Sampled windows are not continuous timetable profiles. See Alternatives, via points, and departure windows.

Result and diagnostics

The public vigo.route.v1 Result contains status, a journey with chronological legs and durations in seconds, warnings, quality, and meta. A not_found Result is a completed answer with journey: null and an access reason when one is known. Read a Result defines every public field.

For a detailed diagnosis, request diagnostics: "trace" and read the internal result under trace. Access failures carry endpoint-specific accessAvailability:

  • outside_selected_budget: an access candidate exists at a larger walking limit. The suggested limit does not guarantee a complete itinerary; streetPathVerified records whether its path was verified.
  • street_access_unverified: nearby stops exist, but the bounded street search did not verify access. nearestStop.distanceKind: "straight_line" describes proximity, not walking distance.
  • none_within_probe: no access candidate was found within probeWalkKm. This is a bounded result, not proof of disconnection at every distance.
  • diagnostic_unavailable: the explanatory probe failed, reported as access_diagnostic_unavailable.

The diagnosis never raises the walking allowance by itself. Blocked plans keep searchLimits for walking, horizon, transfers, and the transit-ride requirement, including horizonScope: "timetable_scan". no_path means no scheduled itinerary under those constraints on the selected date; changing a constraint requires a new query.

Stations, access, and geometry

Anonymous coordinate endpoints and physical GTFS stops use the same nearest-street attachment in Route and Matrix. A parent station does not provide free movement between all its platforms. Declared station paths keep their direction and time; their complete time and distance frontier is prepared once and then filtered against each endpoint's remaining walking budget. Interior pathway nodes do not create extra street entrances.

When GTFS omits traversal_time, the walking policy prices the declared pathway length, or the distance between stop coordinates if length is also absent. Stairs with a stair count and fare or exit gates use labeled estimates described in walking evidence, floored by any available walking distance. A missing time is never a zero-time link. Endpoint walks that use a station path expose accessCost.street and accessCost.station separately, including directed stopIds and source types; this supports a source-data audit, not certification of physical station access.

The walking limit covers each complete, continuous access or egress walk; a transfer walk cannot extend the final egress beyond that budget. Street transfers use declared entrances and directed station pathways, composed around at most one external transfer edge. A repeated station in a ride sequence is reported but not rejected, because a scheduled loop or a forbidden platform change can require it.

A coordinate that snaps to the street graph can carry an endpointConnector on its first or last walking leg. Its coordinates and distance describe the snap already included in the leg's cost, with source: "coordinate-snap" and streetPathVerified: false. A connector is not evidence of a mapped or legally traversable street. For geometry materialization and identifier internals, see itinerary geometry.

Routing

Matrix

2 min readSource

On this page

Send a matrix requestRead the resultChoose constraintsShare work across pairs

Matrix calculates travel time between sets of origins and destinations in one request, from a shared departure time or to a common arrival deadline. Request journeys only when you need their steps. The Matrix request reference lists every field.

Send a matrix request

JSON
{
  "origins": [{"id": "home", "stopId": "A"}],
  "destinations": [{"id": "work", "stopId": "B"}],
  "serviceDate": "2026-10-05",
  "time": "08:30",
  "timePreference": "arrive_by",
  "mode": "transit",
  "includeJourneys": false
}

Replace A and B with exact stop IDs in your City, or use "coordinate": [lon, lat] points; Walk and Drive matrices require coordinates. The quickstart has a complete four-pair Boston example.

Read the result

durationsSeconds[originIndex][destinationIndex] gives each pair's elapsed time, and the ordered endpoints are echoed in query. A null cell means unreachable, never a zero-minute journey; a completed matrix can contain both. With includeJourneys: true, journeys has the same shape with a journey or null per pair. Add includeGeometry: true for path geometry; it requires journeys and performs no extra timetable search.

For arrive-by, a scalar duration is the deadline minus the latest feasible departure. A nested journey reports its actual arrival and may be shorter if it arrives early. Use the journey to separate travel from waiting at the destination. Public durations are seconds; minute-valued rows and search counters appear only in explicitly requested trace output.

Choose constraints

The Route rules apply: a feasible direct walk competes unless requireTransitRide: true, maxWalkKm bounds endpoint walking, maxTransfers accepts 0–31, and horizonMinutes bounds the timetable search rather than the door-to-door duration. allowStreetTransfers, minimumTransferBufferMinutes, and arrivalBufferMinutes behave as described under Route.

Transit Matrix is scheduled. Drive Matrix can use a supplied traffic snapshot with routingDataMode: "realtime"; it never fetches a provider or models traffic changing during a journey. See Street routing.

Share work across pairs

Results keep input order, including repeated endpoints. The compiler accepts up to 100,000 pairs in a 16 MiB request; the engine accepts up to 65,536 pairs in an 8 MiB request. Group work by shared endpoint, date, clock, and constraints:

WorkloadShared timetable search
Depart-at, one origin and many destinationsOne forward scan
Depart-at, many originsOne forward scan per unique origin
Arrive-by, many origins and one destinationOne reverse scan
Arrive-by, many destinationsOne reverse scan per unique destination

Request scalar output when only times are needed. Journey queries also share boarding rounds within each endpoint group, so tied journeys can differ from Route's stable order while satisfying the same objectives. disableCache: true bypasses endpoint-frontier caches while keeping same-request sharing, loaded City data, and immutable street indexes; it does not clear the operating system's page cache. Service benchmarking shows how to measure full caller wall time.

Routing

Reach and isochrones

4 min readSource

On this page

Send a Reach requestSet the analysis resolutionChoose the outputCompare with R5 and OTPInspect a destination in StudioCompare service changes

Reach finds the streets and areas reachable from one origin within a time budget, by scheduled transit with walking or by walking alone. Arrive-by Reach asks the reverse: from where a destination can be reached by a deadline. It does not measure access to jobs or people unless your analysis adds those opportunities. The Reach request reference lists every field.

Send a Reach request

JSON
{
  "origin": {"coordinate": [-71.11902, 42.37334]},
  "serviceDate": "2026-10-05",
  "time": "08:00",
  "mode": "transit",
  "cutoffsMinutes": [15, 30, 45],
  "extentRadiusKm": 6,
  "rasterSize": 96,
  "surfaceSampling": "street"
}
Shell
vigo reach --city ./boston --request reach.json --output reach-result.json

mode: "walk" requests walking-only Reach and needs no service date. Drive and realtime Reach are unavailable. Planned transit changes use transit with street sampling.

For arrive-by Reach, send a destination instead of the origin, with "timePreference": "arrive_by" and the deadline as time. Each value is how long before the deadline a traveler must leave that place, including any wait after an early arrival. Walking keeps each street's permitted direction toward the destination. The Node and Rust CLIs and Python send this same request, and all run Reach in the vigo executable.

Set the analysis resolution

OptionMeaning
cutoffsMinutesTime budgets from 1 to 240 minutes; fractional values are accepted
maxWalkKmTransit walking budget
walkSpeedKphWalking speed from 1 to 8 km/h
extentRadiusKmRequested raster extent from 1 to 40 km
rasterSizeCells per side; the compiler accepts 48, 64, 96, 128, 192, 256, 384, 512, or 1024, and the engine any integer from 16 to 1024
surfaceSamplingstreet samples reached street intervals; cell-center routes to each cell's center

The extent sets the analytical grid; it is not a maximum trip distance. Time budgets, walking limits, and the network decide what is reachable. Keep extent, resolution, sampling, and constraints identical when comparing results.

Choose the output

The default reachFormat: "full" returns the requested grid and the full reached extent. surface.valuesSeconds is row-major from the northwest corner, and null means unreached; read its bounds and dimensions with the values. fullSurface describes the separate full extent when available.

areas are GeoJSON polygons around reachable cells, preserving holes and islands. contours interpolate the sampled times and close at the grid edge and no-data boundaries; diagonal-only cells remain disconnected. The raw raster stays the reference for numerical analysis. For a map, request reachFormat: "map" to receive only the full reached-area polygons and their bounds, without raster values, stop lists, or duplicate contours; map output cannot be compared.

For network evidence, add includeStreetEdges: true (--street-edges on the command line) to the full output. Returned directed intervals keep their explicitly named units. See Reach output for raster ordering and edge decoding.

Compare with R5 and OTP

Use surfaceSampling: "cell-center" for a coordinate-destination surface. The default street mode records the earliest reached street portion in each cell and leaves cells away from reached edges empty; a filled street cell does not establish a route to its center. Area metrics sum sampled cells and do not measure physically walkable land.

When comparing engines, match the origin, service date, departure time, modes, walking and transfer rules, cutoff, extent, and grid resolution before drawing polygons. VIGO Reach evaluates a fixed departure. Conveyal's R5 can aggregate a departure window at a chosen percentile, and OTP's Travel Time API provides a departure-time snapshot; match the temporal statistic first. VIGO raster values are seconds, while requests use cutoffsMinutes.

For quantitative agreement, compute travel times at the same coordinates with Matrix, then classify them at the same cutoff. A longitude/latitude grid and a Web Mercator grid do not share cell centers. Compare contours separately from cell polygons, and check station entrance costs, boarding slack, and GTFS transfer minimums in representative journeys. For a Transit Matrix control that matches Reach's walking budget, set requireTransitRide: false and allowLongWalk: false. See Conveyal's isochrone methodology, OTP's Travel Time API, and the GTFS minimum-transfer rules.

Inspect a destination in Studio

After running Reach in Analyze, click a destination to see its map estimate and request a journey there; with the map focused, press Enter to inspect its center. The journey keeps the analysis origin, date, departure time, timetable selection, and walking and ride limits. Expand Show journey for the walking and transit legs. A missing raster sample does not by itself mean no journey exists.

With street sampling, the Studio map also shades the land between reached streets. Each cell enclosed by the reached network takes its fastest nearby reached street plus a straight walk of up to 100 m, never across mapped water. Land farther than that from a reached street, outside the reached network, or in a City without complete water coverage stays unshaded. The inspector labels these values as off-street estimates. Shading is for display only: area metrics and the saved raster keep the street samples.

Destination journeys use scheduled service and the City's routing walking speed. Planned service changes affect the scenario map estimate but are not reconstructed in the destination journey; the panel labels the difference.

After an Arrive by Reach, the clicked place is where the journey starts: the panel requests an arrive-by journey from it to the destination by the same deadline and counts its time from leaving to the deadline, as the map does.

Compare service changes

Run a baseline, then a planned Scenario with the same origin, clock, date, walking assumptions, sampling, and grid, and retain both Results. Scenarios explains exclusions and added service; Compare saved results explains the counts. A polygon describes modeled network reach. It does not certify entrance access, wheelchair connectivity, pedestrian permissions, or observed reliability; keep the walking evidence and known limits with the analysis.

Routing

Scenarios

4 min readSource

On this page

Planned serviceReplace a branch and keep its tripsSet a frequency insteadEdit a shared edge in StudioCompare the change

A Scenario is an immutable set of changes tied to exactly one City revision. It may contain planned transit service changes, one live transit state, or one supplied traffic state. Walking limits, speeds, departure times, and cutoffs stay query options.

Scenarios never edit the imported GTFS or OSM, and a complete alternative feed is another City revision. Drawing geometry in an editor creates no computational change until it is attached to a valid service edit. Several nonconflicting planned changes may coexist; conflicts need an explicit resolution. A Scenario never moves to another City revision, and expired live state cannot be queried.

In VIGO 1.0.0-rc.2, planned service changes apply to Reach, supplied traffic to Drive Route and Drive Matrix, and supplied realtime predictions to transit Route. Transit Matrix and Reach remain scheduled. Studio can also route transit journeys on a saved scenario, on the scheduled timetable. Unsupported combinations are rejected with an explanation. The Scenario request reference lists every field.

Planned service

A planned service change states what changes and supplies enough to run it: ordered stops, travel-time assumptions, and a departure schedule. Edits to existing branches keep their GTFS trips by default; new service specifies frequency and operating hours. A Reach request can include this scenario:

JSON
{
  "origin": {"coordinate": [-77.05, 38.90]},
  "serviceDate": "2026-07-15",
  "time": "08:00",
  "scenario": {
    "id": "crosstown",
    "name": "Crosstown service",
    "services": [{
      "operation": "add",
      "name": "Crosstown",
      "stops": [
        {"label": "West", "coordinate": [-77.05, 38.90]},
        {"label": "East", "coordinate": [-77.03, 38.91]}
      ],
      "headwayMinutes": 10,
      "startMinutes": 300,
      "endMinutes": 1500,
      "averageSpeedKph": 22
    }],
    "excludedRouteIds": ["route-to-remove"]
  }
}

operation is add, augment, or replace. excludedRouteIds removes selected scheduled route variants for the Scenario.

Replace a branch and keep its trips

replace defaults to scheduleMode: "preserve-trips" and needs sourceRouteId, sourcePatternId, and selected-branch scope (routeScope: "pattern", or omitted when a pattern is supplied). Studio and the compiler load the trips active on the query's service date, including calendar exceptions and departures after midnight. Each affected trip produces exactly one replacement, keeping irregular gaps, per-trip running times, dwell, and pickup and drop-off restrictions. Editing stops never adds departures or reverse service. Older replacement requests use the same default: headway and hour fields are ignored unless frequency mode is selected explicitly.

For a branch that keeps its trips, road geometry distributes each trip's original A → B running time among the edited gaps. Original dwell remains at retained stops, and addedStopDwellMinutes (default 0.35) adds dwell at inserted stops; removing an intermediate stop removes its dwell. The first retained GTFS stop anchors departure timing: a preceding extension departs earlier, and later edits shift downstream times. At least one original stop must remain, with baselineStopId or baselineStopIndex identifying moved stops and repeated visits. An extension requiring a departure before the service date is rejected. These are modeled timing changes, not a vehicle or crew scheduling check.

Set a frequency instead

To change the timetable deliberately, use scheduleMode: "frequency" with headwayMinutes, startMinutes, and endMinutes; Studio calls this Departures → Set frequency and hours. This mode can replace a whole route, and add and augment use it by default. New lines use segmentDistancesKm and averageSpeedKph for road timing, plus dwellMinutes; segment arrays have one value per stop pair. Reverse service is an explicit choice in frequency mode and is never inferred from a shared route name.

Edit a shared edge in Studio

Selected branch only keeps a change on the chosen pattern. All branches serving this exact A → B edge applies one inserted gap to every occurrence of that ordered stop pair within the same feed and public route, but not to the reverse B → A edge. The editor lists the affected branches before running. This scope needs complete branch analysis and one inserted gap; use selected-branch scope for moved stops, extensions, or several gaps. Repeated stop visits keep their own positions and published runtimes, and overlapping replacement services are rejected. Studio requires a completed road path before running a road-following Scenario.

Compare the change

Run a baseline Reach and a Scenario Reach against the same City, origin, date and time, walking policy, cutoffs, and grid, save both, and compare them. Test a planned service change has complete paired requests. Compare reports after-minus-before changes for cells reachable in both surfaces and counts newly and no-longer-reachable cells separately. It checks grid compatibility but not every experiment setting, so read Compare semantics before attributing a mean change to the Scenario.

Routing

Realtime journey routing

4 min readSource

On this page

Two modes, one engineShared timetableAdmission and coverageRead the realtime statusStop predictions and source versionsVerification

Route can use supplied GTFS-Realtime Trip Updates. This chapter explains how predictions are admitted and how to read the outcome; the realtime input reference lists the snapshot fields.

Two modes, one engine

Route exposes routingDataMode: "realtime" | "scheduled", shown in Studio as Realtime and Scheduled · Research. The command-line runtimes default to scheduled and use a supplied realtimeSnapshot; they never fetch feeds. The compiler also accepts --data-mode realtime|scheduled.

Scheduled research requires an explicit service date and time. The server removes realtime and traffic observations before processing, enforces the exact date, and disables date substitution. Studio keeps the selected date and time and ignores feed polling in this mode; live refreshes, expiry checks, and mode changes cancel obsolete realtime requests, and switching modes never shows the other mode's old result.

Both transit modes use the same native algorithms, stop identities, walking and transfer policies, and coordinate search; only the timetable presented to the engine differs. Transit Matrix and Reach remain scheduled and reject realtime requests.

Results for an explicit mode include diagnostics.routingDataMode and routingDataProvenance: source timetable and street identity, service date and timezone, query time, walking and search settings, engine contract version, and a reproducibility key. Realtime results also identify the prediction snapshot, and ordered journeys reject changed data identities between legs. The manifest identifies inputs but does not archive them; retain the City, the VIGO build, the request, and the returned diagnostics to reproduce a result.

Shared timetable

A journey search compiles the complete supplied TripUpdate snapshot into a separate resident timetable. Within the explicit resource limits there is no endpoint-based selection, inspection pruning, or duplicate-stop overlay, and an oversized snapshot is rejected as a whole rather than truncated. Each valid matched update replaces its scheduled trip; canceled and deleted trips lose their ride segments; unreported trips keep scheduled times.

Depart-at, arrive-by, transfer limits, and departure-window alternatives all use this timetable with the existing native algorithms. A query freezes its observation clock, including recursive verification and window samples. The latest compiled snapshot is cached per immutable service kernel and invalidated when input or timestamp validity changes; scheduled queries never inherit predictions from an earlier request.

Admission and coverage

An update must identify an active trip on the selected service day and source scope. Ambiguous identities, contradictory duplicates, invalid timing, unsupported relationships, and stale observations are excluded and counted. Feed and record timestamps are checked independently: admission accepts timestamps at most 180 seconds old and at most 60 seconds ahead of the captured clock. Network tools may apply their own freshness policy first, keeping all rejection counts.

An unreported scheduled prefix may conflict with the first explicit prediction of an early-running trip. The resolver excludes that prefix only when all its departures and the first explicit prediction precede the frozen observation boundary, with no earlier explicit update or trip-level delay. pastPrefixTrips and omittedPastPrefixStops disclose the exclusion; it does not reconstruct past events or claim actual passage.

diagnostics.realtimeRouting identifies the snapshot and counts applied, canceled, stale, unmatched, wrong-date, duplicate, invalid, and unsupported records. coverage accounts for every supplied record, including those rejected before routing. partial means some updates were applied while others were excluded, and failedFeeds reports unavailable endpoints. A scheduled fallback is identified explicitly; compile or search failures never silently retry against scheduled service.

Processing a full snapshot is not a claim that every trip has a prediction. Added, unscheduled, replacement, and duplicated trips without a supported scheduled instance remain unsupported and disclosed. Vehicle positions and text alerts never invent stop-time predictions. Studio's added-service display is separate from routing admission.

Read the realtime status

For transit Route, read diagnostics.realtimeRouting.status together with its counts. routingDataMode: "realtime" records the requested mode; it does not mean that predictions changed the timetable.

StatusMeaning
appliedMatched trip replacements were applied, possibly with cancellations, and no supplied update was rejected
cancellations_onlyOnly trip removals were applied, and no supplied update was rejected
partialAt least one replacement or cancellation was applied and at least one supplied update was rejected
stale_fallbackNo update was applied and feed or record timestamp checks failed
no_matchesNo update was applied for other reasons; check unmatched, wrong-date, duplicate, invalid, and unsupported counts
scheduled_fallbackNo realtime search diagnostics were available; read fallbackReason

coverage.complete concerns admission of the supplied updates; it does not measure the share of scheduled trips that report. A fully admitted cancellation snapshot can legitimately return no journey. routingDataProvenance.realtimeApplied counts both replacements and cancellations. Keep these fields with the answer; see Keep uncertainty with the answer.

Stop predictions and source versions

A trip-level delay propagates forward until a stop-specific prediction replaces it, and a prediction at an intermediate stop never becomes a delay for earlier calls. Absolute time takes precedence over delay; arrival and departure remain separate. NO_DATA resets propagated delay, and SKIPPED removes boarding and alighting while keeping through travel. Repeated stops need an unambiguous sequence, and out-of-order sequences are rejected.

Each decoded record keeps its endpoint, source timestamp, and static-feed scope. VIGO does not compare GTFS-RT feed_version with static feed_info.feed_version, so connect the matching timetable edition yourself. A missing Trip Update means no reported prediction, not verified on-time operation.

Resource admission is separate from semantic coverage. Downloads are bounded, the decoder rejects feeds above 100,000 entities or 500,000 stop predictions, and native reconstruction checks its estimated memory against the timetable budget. Over-limit data is rejected, never silently truncated.

Verification

npm run check:gtfs runs the full feed and routing suite, including more than 256 updated trips, 1,024 input records, and 4,096 updated stops, interior transfers, both time directions, cancellations, skipped stops, transfer limits, snapshot replacement, and timestamp expiry. check-realtime-scheduled-parity.mjs compares 1,536 paired engine queries against eight independently imported GTFS timetables containing the literal effective predictions. check-realtime-past-prefix.mjs and check-routing-data-modes.mjs cover excluded prefixes and observation isolation. These establish algorithm parity for the tested cases, not field ETA accuracy.
