Service benchmarking
4 min readSource
On this page
Explicit linked tripsRealtime replacement trips
Use a retained NDJSON request file containing public Route, Matrix, and Reach requests. Each line includes kind, the City or scenario selection supported by your service, the service date, and all routing constraints. Keep the file and prepared City together with their source checksums.


Shell
node scripts/benchmark-service.mjs \
  --url http://127.0.0.1:8080 \
  --requests queries.ndjson --output results.json \
  --rounds 20 --concurrency 4 --warmup 1 --city ./city


Set VIGO_API_TOKEN if the service requires authentication. The benchmark does not write the token to its report and refuses to overwrite an existing result. It calls the service's /v1/route, /v1/matrix, and /v1/reach endpoints.


The report retains every measured call, warmup calls, request-file hash, runtime capabilities, client platform, and optional unique-file City storage. Latency includes queueing, HTTP, response transfer, and JSON parsing. Quantiles use nearest rank. Successful results, valid no-journey results, HTTP failures, overload, service unavailability, timeouts, invalid responses, and transport failures are reported separately. Errors during warmup also fail the run.


For a cold-start measurement, start a fresh service and use --warmup 0 --rounds 1. Measure readiness separately from the first query. For sustained use, retain the same workload and increase rounds; report how much the workload repeats and whether caches are enabled. Compare equivalent inputs, constraints, output detail, hardware limits, and runtime builds.


City storage counts each file identity once, including shared scenario directories. It is logical file size, not physical APFS clone allocation. Server memory must be measured at the service: retain process-tree RSS/PSS or cgroup memory samples at startup, first query, repeated and concurrent queries, scenario switches, and peak large-output requests. Include the full application stack when claiming a deployment budget. The benchmark client's memory is not server memory.


Use public synthetic fixtures for CI and caller-owned Cities for operational acceptance. A short replay establishes behavior for that retained workload; it does not establish production reliability across unobserved traffic. See upgrading for installation and rollback checks.


Explicit linked trips


The optional trip_links SQLite table preserves from_trip_id, to_trip_id, and transfer_type (4 or 5), including feed namespaces. Existing Cities without it remain readable. A City whose importer discarded these rows must be rebuilt from the original GTFS; no runtime can recover the missing evidence.


The Rust runtime compiles active, chronological type 4 chains once per timetable view, after realtime updates. Splitting and coupling produce bounded through paths. Original trips remain available for partial journeys and for reconstructing source trip IDs, shapes, headsigns and service dates. No new search algorithm or JavaScript routing path is introduced. Ordinary Cities have no extra connection arrays; linked paths add only their own connections. Limits (512 trips per path, 200,000 paths, and four times the original segment count with a 100,000-segment floor) fail explicitly rather than truncate results. Path retention is also capped at one million trip references. Before copying columns, an estimate including spare vector capacity, physical-part copies and name tables must fit one eighth of detected memory capacity, capped at 128 MiB. This bounds estimated additional allocations; it is not a process RSS guarantee.


A public transit leg following an in-seat continuation has continuation: { "type": "stay_aboard", "durationSeconds": 300 }, for example. The duration is the actual onboard gap before that leg, including zero; it is part of journey riding time, not waiting for another vehicle. Transfer limits apply to boardings, not the number of displayed source-trip legs. Boarding or alighting restrictions at the boundary do not force passengers off the vehicle. Through-journey fares remain unavailable where the fare catalog cannot describe the corresponding fare-leg joins; VIGO does not invent an additional or free fare.


Explicit links may connect different terminal stops: the interval between the first trip's arrival and the next trip's departure is onboard movement or dwell. It is included in riding time, without inventing a passenger walking leg. Overlapping clocks, canceled/truncated endpoints and inactive trips do not establish continuity.


The optional trip_operations table retains block identifiers and bicycle permissions. Rust infers consecutive same-terminal block continuations only within one service ID and service day. Adjacency comes from the original schedule, so cancellation cannot skip over a missing middle trip. Explicit links (including type 5) take precedence. Different-terminal blocks and blocks spanning different service IDs still need explicit links. Old Cities without these optional tables retain their existing behavior.


node test/check-linked-trips.mjs checks raw-GTFS import, forward/reverse Route, Matrix, Reach, source identities, dwell, boarding restrictions, realtime, branching and scenario exclusions. The native unit tests cover service-day boundaries and invalid continuity.


Realtime replacement trips


GTFS Realtime REPLACEMENT (experimental, enum value 5) replaces a known trip's complete stop sequence in Rust. Every call must identify an unambiguous existing City stop and an increasing stop sequence, with absolute arrival/departure clocks at every call. Changed intermediate stops and realtime pickup/drop-off restrictions are supported. Incomplete, backwards or unknown-stop replacements are rejected and reported in realtime diagnostics. NEW and DUPLICATED still need new trip identity construction and are not supported by this replacement path.
